https://www.baltictimes.com/estonia_supp.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Estonia supports Latvia in fight against illegal migration - Taro 2026-07-22 LETA/BNS/TBT Staff TALLINN - Minister of the Interior Igor Taro, during a two-day visit to Latvia, received an overview of the country's crisis preparedness, refugee policy, and the situation at its external border, pledging Estonia's support in the fight against illegal migration. The meetings also focused on cooperation between Estonia and Latvia in combating organized crime and cross-border drug trafficking. Estonia also plays a significant role in curbing illegal immigration: in total, Estonian border guards have helped apprehend 133 illegal migrants on Latvia's border with Russia and Belarus. According to Taro, Latvia is one of Estonia's most important partners in the security field. "Latvia is not only Estonia's closest neighbor but also one of our most reliable allies. The cooperation between our law enforcement agencies is practical and effective, based on mutual trust and common goals," the interior minister said. On Tuesday, the delegation reviewed border security on the Latvia-Belarus border. According to Taro, the situation for Latvia is considerably more tense compared to Estonia, and the struggle to prevent illegal border crossings has unfortunately become routine. "The Latvians' experience in dealing with malicious attacks is invaluable, and our police colleagues benefit from it occasionally when we send our personnel to assist them during major malicious incidents. This cooperation will continue," Taro said. As an important part of the visit, Minister Taro visited the disaster management center in Salacgriva, which is one of the first centers to be completed in a nationwide network being established in Latvia. The purpose of these centers is to consolidate rescue, police, border guard, ambulance, and other critical services under one roof to improve preparedness for natural disasters, technological accidents, climate risks, and security crises. The meetings included an overview of the implementation of the joint Estonian-Latvian action plan for combating cross-border drug trafficking and organized crime. According to Taro, the action plan is being successfully implemented, and cooperation covers both strategic and operational levels. "Unfortunately, we face common challenges here, but we are certainly ready to continue our close cooperation." In addition, the Estonian Minister of the Interior familiarized himself with the operations of an asylum center in Latvia and the services provided to applicants for international protection. Share it with your friends! Facebook Twitter Google Pinterest Reddit Email LinkedIn Timișoara mayor Dominic Fritz will remain in office but have his salary reduced by 10% for six months following a final court ruling that found him in an administrative conflict of interest, Timiș prefect Paul Finta announced on Tuesday, August 4. The sanction has sparked a new political dispute between USR and the Social Democratic Party (PSD), with Fritz accusing the Social Democrats of campaigning to remove him from office and PSD arguing that his mandate should have been terminated. In June, Romania's High Court of Cassation and Justice upheld a Timișoara Court of Appeal ruling that found Dominic Fritz in an administrative conflict of interest. “I signed the order applying the disciplinary sanction of reducing the allowance by 10% for a period of six months to Dominic Fritz, the mayor of Timișoara," Paul Finta said at a press conference, according to News.ro . The Timiș prefect further stated that he had requested an opinion from the National Integrity Agency (ANI) but had not received a response. He also pointed to an ANI announcement saying the agency currently has 122 conflict-of-interest cases under consideration and that none has resulted in the termination of a mayor's mandate. Dominic Fritz, the president of Save Romania Union (USR), who remains in office following the prefect's decision, reacted by saying he accepted the sanction but maintained that the case against him was unfair. “I take note of this sanction with my head held high. The law and justice are not always the same thing," Fritz wrote on Facebook. According to the mayor, the conflict-of-interest finding concerns his decision to submit for a vote in the Timișoara Local Council an urban zoning plan, or PUZ, that had been drafted entirely before he took office. Fritz then accused PSD of conducting a campaign against him and the mandate he received from Timișoara voters. “The campaign carried out by PSD, which controls ANI and part of the judiciary, against the vote of Timișoara residents for mayor has become far too obvious," he said. Dominic Fritz also argued that a PSD prefect in Timiș County had imposed the same sanction - a reduction in salary - on the PSD mayor of Recaș in 2023 after the latter was found in a conflict of interest. He further accused the Social Democrats of now seeking to change the law to introduce the termination of a mayor's mandate as a sanction in such cases. PSD responded by challenging the prefect's interpretation of the law and calling on ANI and the Interior Ministry to contest his order before an administrative court, Agerpres reported. The Social Democrats argued that Fritz's mandate should have ended following the final court ruling and accused USR representatives of attempting to protect their party leader from the legal consequences of the conflict-of-interest finding. PSD cited a 2020 High Court decision which, according to the party's interpretation, establishes that the mandates of local elected officials definitively found to be incompatible or in a conflict of interest terminate by operation of law. “PSD asks the National Integrity Agency and the Interior Ministry to urgently intervene against this abuse and challenge the Timiș prefect's illegal order before the administrative court," the party said, as quoted by Agerpres. The party also called on prosecutors to open a criminal investigation into USR representatives over what it described as the abusive use of public offices to shield Fritz from the sanctions it believes should apply. irina.marica@romania-insider.com (Photo source: Inquam Photos/Virgil Simonescu) Read next 19 June 2026 Justice Romania’s High Court rules that Timișoara mayor Dominic Fritz is in a conflict of interest Normal Politics Timișoara mayor Dominic Fritz gets six-month salary cut over conflict of interest ruling, sparking new political row 05 August 2026 Irina Marica Like this article? https://www.budapesttimes.hu/hungary/mir.text: The Budapest Times Mirror, mirror: president calls for Hungary to face its reflection It is important for a nation to know its past, its values, and to be able to see itself through the eyes of others, the President of the Republic said at the University of Miskolc at the ceremonial opening of the 9th International Hungarological Congress on Monday. In his address, András Baka highlighted that self-knowledge gains importance in times of rapid political, social, and cultural change. He noted that the study of the image of Hungarians is one of the important sources of national self-knowledge. In his view, the image that forms of the nation in the world, and the historical experiences, cultural encounters, or misunderstandings that have shaped it, also brings Hungarians closer to a more precise understanding of themselves. András Baka stressed that the image of Hungarians is not merely a heritage but an achievement — one that, alongside cultural and scientific accomplishments, can also be shaped by the way the nation is present in the world as Hungarians. He added that this also carries responsibility: that what Hungarians inherit should be preserved, understood, enriched, and passed on. The President of the Republic remarked that the freedom of science and the meeting of different perspectives are indispensable for this. He stressed that genuine scientific dialogue must make room for debate, since — as he put it — questions and differing viewpoints can bring people closer to “a more important understanding.” In his view, criticism can fulfil its true role when it encourages people to think and helps them examine what they are researching or interpreting in a more nuanced way and from a different perspective. As President of the Republic, he said he considers it important to support — through diplomatic means — every initiative that serves to preserve and enrich the nation’s shared values. András Baka emphasised that the time horizon of science extends beyond a single human lifetime, and that every uncovered source, new discovery, and preserved memory adds something to the knowledge that people pass on to the next generation. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Kayden Tran, 18, a Canley Vale high school student, after finishing his first HSC exam of 2026. Photograph: Teagan Glenane/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Kayden Tran, 18, a Canley Vale high school student, after finishing his first HSC exam of 2026. Photograph: Teagan Glenane/The Guardian Australia news Bacon, eggs and Bowie: how year 12 English students tackled ‘human strength and vulnerability’ in HSC paper Tens of thousands of high school students across New South Wales sit the first test of their final exams Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Nick Visser Tue 13 Oct 2026 02.56 EDT Last modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 03.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google “How does the composer of your prescribed text offer you opportunities to examine assumptions about human strength and vulnerability?” This was the bamboozling English question tens of thousands of year 12 students sat down to answer on the first day of their final school exams. Kayden Tran, 18, had a “really great breakfast” of rice, bacon and eggs – but was it enough to get through an essay exploring tenacity and sensitivity in the writings of Tim Winton, George Orwell or Malala Yousafza? “This morning, I felt extremely stressed and I kind of gave up hope,” the student of Canley Vale high school in Sydney’s west told the Guardian. “But after doing the exam, I feel perfectly fine, I feel content, like I did the best I possibly could,” he said after the HSC English 1 paper on Tuesday. Mary Alnimry listened to the song Heroes by the late David Bowie to prepare. “I discovered that song through an assessment for year 10 and, every time, before every English exam, I listen to that song and it just reminds me of English,” she said. The pair was among about 200 Canley Vale students to sit the test, just one cohort in the roughly 75,000 students across New South Wales working to wrap up their high school careers. “You just have to go in and believe that you know the content,” Alnimry, 17, said. “That’s how I felt in the morning. And then after the exam, obviously it’s really rewarding. I completed everything, but there’s always that curiosity lingering. “I think that it was pretty fair, there was nothing out of the ordinary.” View image in fullscreen Canley Vale high school students finishing their first HSC English exam of 2026. Photograph: Teagan Glenane/The Guardian On Reddit, other year 12 students weren’t as confident. “Honestly I think that’ll kick most people in the ass, the fact the question had so much to unpack I personally found it hard to address it all, I focused on vulnerability and strength and sprinkled a bit of assumptions,” one student with the handle bberson wrote on Tuesday afternoon. Another, djungleskog41, was concerned they skipped over parts of the question: “I did Orwell too and tbh I didn’t address the question at all. I only focused on how like human vulnerability and weakness forces us to submit into the regime and rebelling is a sign of human strength blah blah blah but i barely mentioned my assumption so im rlly upset about that lol.” Alana Miller, an English teacher at Canley Vale high school, has shepherded 17 years of year 12 students through the exams. She said the nerves don’t stop with students, and she too woke up this morning with the year 12s on her mind. “We care so much about the students, we spend so much time,” she said. “We want them to do well, we want them to feel particularly that these exams are something they could achieve in.” Fantasy books have been a growing hit at Canley Vale high alongside Japanese manga. Miller said she’s spent the past year trying to meet students where they are to help engage the next generation of readers. “I think the best way is to … talk to them about books, shows, films that they might see,” Miller said. “I think choosing engaging texts in the classroom can be a huge stepping stone for resistant readers. … I just try and tell them they haven’t met the book yet that will get them to love reading.” For Zenith Diep, self-belief was key. “I’m feeling not too bad, because I did finish everything,” the 17-year-old said. “I don’t know if I answered the questions fully as I should’ve. You just have to trust yourself with how much work you put in and that you actually remember it. I trust in myself.” Effie Niarchos, the principal of Canley Vale high, said the HSC represented a rite of passage for year 12s, marking the past six years of high school and the next chapter in their lives. “All of the teaching, all the learning is building towards this moment,” she said. “We want them to be ready for the world, and we look at it as we’ve achieved something to be able to successfully prepare them for this moment”. She said students have been experiencing a bit more anxiety in recent years, possibly from community expectations, possibly from the world shifting underneath kids’ feet. But as she saw off the last of those who sat for the exam on Tuesday, she looked back with a smile and a sense of pride. “They’re our future,” Niarchos said. HSC results will be released on 16 December.
